reason: The supplied proof incorrectly varies \(y\): in the theorem \(y\) is fixed, so divisibility at \(Y=y^{2}\) does not imply polynomial divisibility for all square values of \(Y\). The proof above repairs this gap by fixing each modulus and bounding the multiplicative order of \(x\) modulo it.
text:
Assume, toward a contradiction, that \(x>1\). We use Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.

Fix any positive integer \(n\), and put
\[
M=n^{2}y^{2}+1.
\]
The hypothesis gives \(M\mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1\), so \(\gcd(x,M)=1\). Let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_M(x)\).

If a prime \(p\) satisfies \(p\equiv \pm n\pmod M\), then
\[
p^{2}y^{2}+1\equiv n^{2}y^{2}+1\equiv0\pmod M.
\]
Applying the hypothesis with the index \(p\), and using \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), yields
\[
M\mid p^{2}y^{2}+1\mid x^{p-1}-1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
d\mid p-1. \tag{1}
\]

We show that \(d\mid2\). Let \(\ell\) be an odd prime. If \(\ell\mid M\), choose \(\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}\) such that \(\varepsilon n\not\equiv1\pmod\ell\); such a sign exists because \(\ell\nmid n\) and \(\ell\) is odd. Since \(\gcd(\varepsilon n,M)=1\), Dirichlet’s theorem supplies a prime \(p\equiv\varepsilon n\pmod M\). Then \(\ell\nmid p-1\), so (1) shows that \(\ell\nmid d\).

If instead \(\ell\nmid M\), choose a nonzero residue \(r\not\equiv1\pmod\ell\). By the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem, there is a prime satisfying
\[
p\equiv n\pmod M,\qquad p\equiv r\pmod\ell.
\]
Again (1) gives \(d\mid p-1\), while \(\ell\nmid p-1\); hence \(\ell\nmid d\). Thus \(d\) has no odd prime divisor.

It remains to show that \(4\nmid d\). There is a reduced residue class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(M,4)\) whose elements are congruent to \(n\pmod M\) and to \(3\pmod4\): if \(M\) is odd this follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem, while if \(M\) is even, then \(ny\) is odd and \(M\equiv2\pmod4\), so exactly one of \(n,n+M\) is \(3\pmod4\). Dirichlet’s theorem therefore gives a prime \(p\equiv n\pmod M\) with \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). From (1), \(d\mid p-1\), but \(4\nmid p-1\). Hence \(4\nmid d\).

Therefore \(d\in\{1,2\}\), and hence
\[
x^{2}\equiv1\pmod M.
\]
Since \(n\) was arbitrary,
\[
n^{2}y^{2}+1\mid x^{2}-1
\]
for every positive integer \(n\). Choosing \(n\) so large that \(n^{2}y^{2}+1>x^{2}-1>0\) is impossible. This contradiction eliminates \(x>1\). Since \(x\) is positive, it follows that \(\boxed{x=1}\).
